# AI assistance disclosure

Portions of the R code were produced with
assistance from an AI coding tool. Every chunk was run on the GESS files
in this folder, checked against the printed output, and edited by the
group. The analytical decisions - including the join-key resolution and
the missingness treatment rules - are ours, and each member can defend
them in the viva.

# 1. Introduction and analytical question

This project looks at which student, household and school characteristics
are linked to dropout risk and core-subject performance among JHS and SHS
students in Ghana. We are using the Ghana Education and School Survey
(GESS) dataset, which combines student records with information about the
schools they attend.

Our main outcome is `Dropout_Risk_Score` - a continuous score from 0 to
10 - which we predict using multiple linear regression in Task 5. We also
look at `Passed_Core` (whether a student passed core subjects) as a
secondary outcome for the chi-square test in Task 4 and the
classification model in Task 6. We do not use `Overall_Average` or the
four individual subject scores as predictors of `Passed_Core`, because
`Passed_Core` is defined as `Overall_Average >= 50` - predicting one from
the other would not be a real finding. Task 1 covers importing, joining
and cleaning the two files. Task 2 then prepares the final analysis
dataset.

# 2. Task 1: Data import, joining, and initial inspection

## 2.1 Importing the data (Task 1a)

We start by loading both CSV files using `read_csv()` from the `readr` package (part of
`tidyverse`). Then we use `glimpse()` to see the structure of each file - how many rows and
columns there are, what the column names are, and what type of data is in each column.

```{r import-files}
# load the two datasets
gess_student <- read_csv("gess_student.csv")
gess_school  <- read_csv("gess_school.csv")
```

```{r glimpse-student}
# check the student data
glimpse(gess_student)
```

The student file has `r nrow(gess_student)` rows and `r ncol(gess_student)` columns. Each
row is one student. The `Student_ID` column is a unique identifier for each student, and
`School_ID` links every student to their school. Students in this file come from
`r n_distinct(gess_student$School_ID)` different schools. Most background columns like
`Sex`, `Form_Level`, `Parent_Education`, `HH_Income_Band` and `Passed_Core` are stored as
character type. The numeric columns include subject scores, `Overall_Average`,
`Attendance_Rate_Pct`, `Study_Hours_Day`, `Teacher_Support_Score` and `Dropout_Risk_Score`.
We will use `Dropout_Risk_Score` (a continuous score from 0 to 10) as the primary outcome
for this project, and `Passed_Core` (Yes/No) as the secondary outcome.

The codebook says `Passed_Core` is `Yes` whenever `Overall_Average` is 50 or above. 

```{r check-passed-core}
# check if Passed_Core exactly matches Overall_Average >= 50
gess_student %>%
  mutate(expected = if_else(Overall_Average >= 50, "Yes", "No")) %>%
  count(Passed_Core, expected)
```

Every row in the table is on the diagonal - `Passed_Core` and `Overall_Average >= 50` match
for all `r nrow(gess_student)` students. This means `Passed_Core` is just a recode of
`Overall_Average`, not an independent outcome. We will not use `Overall_Average` or the
four subject scores to predict `Passed_Core` - that would be predicting a variable from
itself.

```{r glimpse-school}
# check the school data
glimpse(gess_school)
```

The school file has `r nrow(gess_school)` rows and `r ncol(gess_school)` columns. Each row
is one school. `School_ID` is the key that connects schools to students. Character columns
describe school characteristics like `School_Type`, `School_Level` and `Urban_Rural`.
Numeric columns include `Total_Enrolment`, `Pupil_Teacher_Ratio`, `Qualified_Teachers_Pct`,
exam pass rates, `Annual_Budget_GHS` and `Resource_Index`. These school-level variables
will be used as predictors of student dropout risk alongside the student-level predictors.

## 2.2 Joining the two files (Task 1b)

### Join key checks

Before joining, we make sure `School_ID` is unique in the school file (so there is exactly
one school record per school) and that every student has a matching school record.

```{r check-school-id-duplicates}
# check if School_ID is duplicated in the school file
gess_school %>%
  count(School_ID) %>%
  filter(n > 1)
```

```{r check-unmatched-students}
# check if any students do not have a matching school
gess_student %>%
  anti_join(gess_school, by = "School_ID")
```

Both checks return empty results. `School_ID` is unique in the school file and every student
has a matching school record, so the join key is clean.

### Left join and justification

We used a left join starting from the student file. The analysis is about students, so we
need to keep all `r nrow(gess_student)` student rows. A left join keeps every row from
the left-hand table (the student file) and adds the matching school information alongside
each student using `School_ID`. An inner join would give the same result here because every
student already has a matching school, but a left join makes the intention clear - we never
want to lose a student row.

```{r join-files}
# join the two datasets - student file on the left
gess_joined <- gess_student %>%
  left_join(gess_school, by = "School_ID", suffix = c("_student", "_school"))

# confirm all students are still there
nrow(gess_joined)
```

The joined file has `r nrow(gess_joined)` rows - exactly the same as the student file, so
no students were lost.

### Handling the duplicate Region column

Both files have a `Region` column. When we joined them, `dplyr` created `Region_student`
(from the student file) and `Region_school` (from the school file). We need to check whether
they agree with each other.

```{r check-region-agreement}
# check how often the two Region columns agree
region_mismatch_count <- sum(gess_joined$Region_student != gess_joined$Region_school,
                             na.rm = TRUE)
region_mismatch_pct   <- round(100 * region_mismatch_count / nrow(gess_joined), 1)

gess_joined %>%
  count(region_match = Region_student == Region_school)
```

The two Region columns disagree for `r region_mismatch_count` of `r nrow(gess_joined)` rows
(`r region_mismatch_pct`%). 
Because the school file is the official record of where each school is located, we use
`school_region` for all geographic analysis. We keep `student_region` in the dataset as
well, so the disagreement remains visible, but we do not use it for any summaries or maps.

```{r rename-region-columns}
# rename both Region columns and set the main Region to the school file's version
gess_joined <- gess_joined %>%
  rename(
    student_region = Region_student,
    school_region  = Region_school
  ) %>%
  mutate(Region = school_region)
```

### First 10 rows of the joined dataset

```{r first-ten-rows}
# look at the first 10 rows
gess_joined %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

The joined dataset has `r nrow(gess_joined)` rows and `r ncol(gess_joined)` columns. The
student count is unchanged, which confirms the left join kept every student.

---

## 2.3 Missing value audit (Task 1c)

### Counting the missing values

We use `colSums(is.na())` to count how many values are missing in every column of the joined
dataset. We also calculate the percentage, using the 2,500 student rows as the denominator.

```{r missing-audit}
# count missing values in each column
missing_before <- tibble(
  Variable   = names(gess_joined),
  Missing    = colSums(is.na(gess_joined))
) %>%
  mutate(Percentage = round(100 * Missing / nrow(gess_joined), 2)) %>%
  arrange(desc(Missing))

missing_before %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Table 2: Missing-value counts for every variable in the joined dataset")
```

```{r variables-with-missing}
# keep only the variables that have at least one missing value
missing_with_nas <- missing_before %>%
  filter(Missing > 0)

missing_with_nas %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Table 3: Variables with missing values only")
```

```{r missing-bar-chart, fig.cap = "Percentage of missing values in each incomplete variable. School-level variables show higher percentages because one missing school record is copied across all students at that school."}
# bar chart of missing values
ggplot(missing_with_nas,
       aes(x = Percentage, y = reorder(Variable, Percentage))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1f4e79", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(Percentage, "%")), hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    title = "Missingness among incomplete variables",
    x     = "Missing (%)",
    y     = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

There are `r nrow(missing_with_nas)` variables with missing values. Several of the
higher-percentage variables - `WASSCE_Pass_Rate_Pct`, `Annual_Budget_GHS`,
`BECE_Pass_Rate_Pct`, `Qualified_Teachers_Pct` and `Pupil_Teacher_Ratio` - are
school-level. One missing school record is copied to every student in that school when the
files are joined, which inflates the student-level percentages. The table below shows the
actual school-level counts, where the denominator is 100 schools, not 2,500 students.

```{r school-level-missing}
# check missing values directly on the 100 schools
gess_school %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(),
               names_to  = "Variable",
               values_to = "Schools_Missing") %>%
  filter(Schools_Missing > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(Schools_Missing)) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Table 4: Missing values on the 100 schools (school-level denominator)")
```

### Treatment decisions

**Dropout_Risk_Score: 100 students (4.0%), Option (i): listwise deletion.**
This is the primary outcome. We do not impute the variable we are trying to predict because
that would create artificial outcome values and could bias the regression results. These rows
are therefore removed when the final analysis dataset is created in Task 2.

**Attendance_Rate_Pct (5.0%), Study_Hours_Day (4.0%), Teacher_Support_Score (3.0%):
Option (iii), group-level median imputation by Form_Level.**
These are continuous predictors with relatively low levels of missingness. The median is used
because it is less affected by extreme values than the mean. Imputing within `Form_Level`
also preserves differences that may exist between students at different stages of schooling.

**HH_Income_Band (5.0%) and Parent_Occupation (4.0%): Option (ii), mode imputation.**
These are categorical variables with relatively low levels of missingness. The mode, which is
the most frequently occurring category, is used because it is the categorical counterpart to
a simple central-value imputation. With only a small proportion of values missing, this
approach retains the observations without introducing a new category that is not present in
the original data.

**Mathematics_Score and Science_Score (4.0% each): Option (iv), retain as NA.**
These subject scores feed directly into `Overall_Average`, which defines `Passed_Core`.
Imputing them would affect the secondary outcome we are analysing. The dropout models do not
use the four subject scores as predictors, so we retain the missing values and use `na.rm = TRUE`
when a summary requires complete observations.

**Pupil_Teacher_Ratio (4 schools), Qualified_Teachers_Pct (5 schools),
Annual_Budget_GHS (6 schools): Option (iii), group-level median imputation by School_Level.**
These are school-level continuous variables. JHS, SHS and Combined schools may differ in
staffing and funding, so a single overall median could mix distinct groups. We therefore impute
within `School_Level` on the school file before joining it back to the student data.

**BECE_Pass_Rate_Pct (5 schools) and WASSCE_Pass_Rate_Pct (8 schools): Option (iv),
retain as NA.**
These exam pass rates are not required as main predictors in the dropout analysis. Retaining
them as `NA` avoids unnecessary imputation, and `na.rm = TRUE` can be used if they are
summarised later.

### Implementing the treatment

We impute the student file and school file separately, then re-join the cleaned files to
create `gess_working`.

```{r impute-student-file}
# helper function: return the most frequent non-missing category
get_mode <- function(x) {
  values <- x[!is.na(x)]
  names(sort(table(values), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
}

# impute the student file
gess_student_imputed <- gess_student %>%
  # use mode imputation for categorical variables with low missingness
  mutate(
    HH_Income_Band = replace_na(HH_Income_Band, get_mode(HH_Income_Band)),
    Parent_Occupation = replace_na(Parent_Occupation, get_mode(Parent_Occupation))
  ) %>%
  # fill continuous predictors with the group median within each Form_Level
  group_by(Form_Level) %>%
  mutate(
    Attendance_Rate_Pct   = replace_na(Attendance_Rate_Pct,
                                       median(Attendance_Rate_Pct,   na.rm = TRUE)),
    Study_Hours_Day       = replace_na(Study_Hours_Day,
                                       median(Study_Hours_Day,       na.rm = TRUE)),
    Teacher_Support_Score = replace_na(Teacher_Support_Score,
                                       median(Teacher_Support_Score, na.rm = TRUE))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```

```{r impute-school-file}
# impute the school file
gess_school_imputed <- gess_school %>%
  # fill school-level numeric variables with the group median within each School_Level
  group_by(School_Level) %>%
  mutate(
    Pupil_Teacher_Ratio    = replace_na(Pupil_Teacher_Ratio,
                                        median(Pupil_Teacher_Ratio,    na.rm = TRUE)),
    Qualified_Teachers_Pct = replace_na(Qualified_Teachers_Pct,
                                        median(Qualified_Teachers_Pct, na.rm = TRUE)),
    Annual_Budget_GHS      = replace_na(Annual_Budget_GHS,
                                        median(Annual_Budget_GHS,      na.rm = TRUE))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```

```{r create-working-dataset}
# re-join the imputed files to create the working dataset for the rest of the project
gess_working <- gess_student_imputed %>%
  left_join(gess_school_imputed, by = "School_ID", suffix = c("_student", "_school")) %>%
  rename(
    student_region = Region_student,
    school_region  = Region_school
  ) %>%
  mutate(Region = school_region)

dim(gess_working)
```

### Before and after comparison

```{r missing-after}
# count missing values in the working dataset
missing_after <- tibble(
  Variable = names(gess_working),
  After    = colSums(is.na(gess_working))
)

# build the before-and-after table for variables that had missing values
missing_comparison <- missing_before %>%
  filter(Missing > 0) %>%
  rename(Before = Missing, Before_Pct = Percentage) %>%
  left_join(missing_after, by = "Variable") %>%
  mutate(Replaced = Before - After) %>%
  select(Variable, Before, Before_Pct, After, Replaced)

missing_comparison %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Table 5: Missing values before and after treatment")
```

```{r total-replaced}
# total number of cells that were filled
total_replaced <- sum(missing_comparison$Replaced, na.rm = TRUE)
```

The treatment filled `r total_replaced` missing cells without removing any student rows at
this stage. `Attendance_Rate_Pct`, `Study_Hours_Day`, `Teacher_Support_Score`,
`Pupil_Teacher_Ratio`, `Qualified_Teachers_Pct` and `Annual_Budget_GHS` were filled with
group medians. `HH_Income_Band` and `Parent_Occupation` were filled using mode imputation,
while `Mathematics_Score`, `Science_Score`, `BECE_Pass_Rate_Pct` and
`WASSCE_Pass_Rate_Pct` are deliberately retained as NA. The 100 students with a missing
`Dropout_Risk_Score` will be removed in Task 2 when we set up the final analysis dataset.

The working dataset `gess_working` has `r nrow(gess_working)` rows and
`r ncol(gess_working)` columns and is ready for Task 2.

# 3. Task 2: Data Wrangling

## 3.1 Variable Selection (Task 2a)

### Analytical question

What student, household, and school characteristics are associated with dropout risk and
core-subject performance among GESS students?

### Outcome variables

The **primary outcome** is `Dropout_Risk_Score` - a continuous score from 0 to 10, where a
higher score means the student is more at risk of dropping out. We use this for the regression
analysis in Task 5 (Pathway A).

The **secondary outcome** is `Passed_Core` - a binary Yes/No variable for whether the student
passed the core subjects (i.e. `Overall_Average >= 50`). We use this in the chi-square test
in Task 4 and the classification model in Task 6.

We do not use `Perf_Band` or `Overall_Average` as modelling targets. `Perf_Band` is just a
bucketed version of `Overall_Average`, and `Passed_Core` is a direct recode of it. Using
them together would be circular.

### Predictor variables

We use the predictors below across all tasks. We need at least three continuous and three
categorical predictors.

**Continuous predictors:**

- `Attendance_Rate_Pct` - attendance rate; low attendance is a direct risk factor for dropping out
- `Study_Hours_Day` - daily study hours outside school; reflects academic effort
- `Teacher_Support_Score` - student's rating of how supported they feel by teachers (1–10)
- `Resource_Index` - a composite measure of school resources (0–10)
- `Pupil_Teacher_Ratio` - students per teacher; higher values mean less individual attention

**Categorical predictors:**

- `HH_Income_Band` - household income group (Low / Mid / High)
- `Parent_Education` - highest education level of the parent or guardian
- `School_Level` - whether the school is JHS, SHS or Combined
- `School_Type` - Public, Private or Mission
- `Sex` - Male or Female
- `Internet_Access_School` - whether the student has internet access at school (Yes/No)
- `Residence_Type` - Day student or Boarder

---

## 3.2 Reshaping the Data (Task 2b)

The four subject scores - `English_Score`, `Mathematics_Score`, `Science_Score` and
`Social_Studies_Score` - are currently stored as four separate columns. In Task 3 we want
to make a faceted box plot that shows the score distribution for each subject side by side,
with separate panels for students who passed and those who did not. That kind of plot needs
`Subject` as a column (not as four separate column names) and `Score` as another column.
We use `pivot_longer()` to reshape the four score columns into rows, creating one row per
student per subject.

We create this as a separate object called `subject_scores_long`. The main analysis dataset stays wide and retains these score columns so that the Task 3 visualisation is derived from the cleaned analysis sample.

---

## 3.3 String Manipulation (Task 2c)

### Operation 1: Extract a numeric student number from Student_ID (str_extract)

`Student_ID` values look like `"GESS-S0001"`. We use `str_extract()` to pull out just the digits and convert them to an integer. The resulting `Student_Num` provides a simpler numeric identifier that can be useful for ordering, labelling and numerical operations in output tables.

```{r string-op1-before}
# what Student_ID looks like before
gess_working %>%
  select(Student_ID) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)
```

```{r string-op1-apply}
# extract the number from Student_ID and convert to integer
gess_working <- gess_working %>%
  mutate(Student_Num = as.integer(str_extract(Student_ID, "\\d+")))
```

```{r string-op1-after}
# check the result
gess_working %>%
  select(Student_ID, Student_Num) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)
```

### Operation 2: Shorten the HH_Income_Band labels (str_remove)

`HH_Income_Band` contains labels like `"Low (<GHS 800)"`, `"Mid (GHS 800-2000)"` and
`"High (>GHS 2000)"`. These long labels will take up too much space on plot axes. We use
`str_remove()` to strip the part in brackets, leaving just `"Low"`, `"Mid"` and `"High"`.
After mode imputation, all values in this variable follow the original category labels, so the same string operation can be applied consistently.

```{r string-op2-before}
# what HH_Income_Band looks like before
gess_working %>%
  count(HH_Income_Band)
```

```{r string-op2-apply}
# remove the bracketed GHS amounts
gess_working <- gess_working %>%
  mutate(HH_Income_Band = str_remove(HH_Income_Band, "\\s*\\(.*\\)"))
```

```{r string-op2-after}
# check the result
gess_working %>%
  count(HH_Income_Band)
```

---

## 3.4 Filtering, Selecting, and Mutating (Task 2d)

### Filter

In Task 1 we decided to apply listwise deletion to `Dropout_Risk_Score` because it is the
primary outcome - filling in the variable we are trying to predict would manufacture the
signal we are then modelling. Here we apply that decision and remove the 100 students with a
missing primary outcome.

```{r check-missing-outcome}
# how many students have a missing Dropout_Risk_Score?
sum(is.na(gess_working$Dropout_Risk_Score))
```

```{r filter-missing-outcome}
# remove those students
n_before_filter <- nrow(gess_working)

dat_clean <- gess_working %>%
  filter(!is.na(Dropout_Risk_Score))

n_removed <- n_before_filter - nrow(dat_clean)

cat("Rows before filter:", n_before_filter, "\n")
cat("Rows removed:      ", n_removed, "\n")
cat("Rows remaining:    ", nrow(dat_clean), "\n")
```

```{r outcome-missing-before-after}
# explicitly show the before/after missing count for the primary outcome
outcome_missing_check <- tibble(
  Stage = c("Before listwise deletion", "After listwise deletion"),
  Missing_Dropout_Risk_Score = c(
    sum(is.na(gess_working$Dropout_Risk_Score)),
    sum(is.na(dat_clean$Dropout_Risk_Score))
  )
)

outcome_missing_check %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Table 6: Missing primary-outcome values before and after listwise deletion.")
```

We removed `r n_removed` students with a missing `Dropout_Risk_Score`. The working dataset
now has `r nrow(dat_clean)` students.

### Select

The joined dataset currently has `r ncol(gess_working)` columns. Many of them are not
needed for the analysis - for example, the school's separate geographic coordinates (`Latitude_S`, `Longitude_S`),
`student_region` (the conflicting region from the student file that we decided not to use
in Task 1), the individual subject scores (which we cannot use as predictors for `Passed_Core`
without leakage), `Overall_Average` (same leakage problem), and school-level exam pass rates
that we kept as NA. We keep the variables directly relevant to the analytical question, including the student coordinates needed for the geographic analysis and the subject scores needed for the required long-format visualisation.

```{r select-variables}
# keep only the variables needed for the analysis
dat_clean <- dat_clean %>%
  select(
    # identifiers and geographic coordinates
    Student_ID, Student_Num, School_ID, Latitude, Longitude,
    # student demographics
    Sex, Age, Form_Level, Residence_Type,
    # household background
    Parent_Education, Parent_Occupation, HH_Income_Band, HH_Size, Orphan_Status,
    # student engagement
    Attendance_Rate_Pct, Study_Hours_Day, Has_Textbooks_All,
    Internet_Access_School, Bullying_Experienced,
    # school quality
    Teacher_Support_Score,
    # school context
    School_Level, School_Type, Urban_Rural, Region,
    # school resources
    Resource_Index, Pupil_Teacher_Ratio,
    # subject scores retained for Task 3 visualisation only
    English_Score, Mathematics_Score, Science_Score, Social_Studies_Score,
    # outcomes
    Passed_Core, Dropout_Risk_Score, Perf_Band
  )

# check dimensions
dim(dat_clean)
```

We kept `r ncol(dat_clean)` variables - more than the 15 required.

### Mutate

**Operation 1 - New continuous variable: Attendance_Gap**

We create `Attendance_Gap` as `100 - Attendance_Rate_Pct`. This is the percentage of school
days a student missed. It re-expresses attendance as absence rather than presence, which
maps more directly to dropout risk. A student who attended 70% of days missed 30%, and that
30% is what puts them at risk. Because `Attendance_Gap` is calculated directly from `Attendance_Rate_Pct`, the two variables contain the same information and should not be used together as regression predictors. `Attendance_Gap` is therefore created for interpretation and visualisation rather than alongside `Attendance_Rate_Pct` in the regression model.

**Operation 2 - New categorical variable: Risk_Level (case_when)**

We split `Dropout_Risk_Score` into three named groups using `case_when()`. In this dataset
the score only goes up to 6.9 (not the full 0–10 described in the codebook), so we use
thresholds of 2 and 4 that give three reasonably sized groups. `Risk_Level` is easier to
read in bar charts and cross-tabulations in Task 3 and Task 4 than the raw score.

**Operation 3 - Factor ordering**

We convert all categorical columns to factors with the correct level order. This matters
because R plots categories in level order, and regression models pick the first level as
the baseline. For variables with a natural progression (like `Perf_Band` and
`HH_Income_Band`) the order goes from lowest to highest so that any effect we estimate
reflects an increase.

```{r mutate-operations}
dat_clean <- dat_clean %>%
  mutate(

    # --- operation 1: new continuous - percentage of school days missed ---
    Attendance_Gap = 100 - Attendance_Rate_Pct,

    # --- operation 2: new categorical - three-group dropout risk level ---
    # Note: the score only reaches 6.9 in this dataset, not the full 0-10 range.
    # Thresholds of 2 and 4 give three workable groups for visualisation.
    Risk_Level = case_when(
      Dropout_Risk_Score <= 2.0 ~ "Low",
      Dropout_Risk_Score <= 4.0 ~ "Medium",
      Dropout_Risk_Score >  4.0 ~ "High"
    ),
    Risk_Level = factor(Risk_Level, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")),

    # --- operation 3: factor ordering and categorical cleanup ---
    Perf_Band = factor(Perf_Band,
                       levels = c("Below Average", "Average", "Good", "Excellent")),
    Parent_Education = factor(Parent_Education,
                              levels = c("None", "Primary", "JHS", "SHS", "Tertiary"),
                              ordered = TRUE),
    HH_Income_Band = factor(HH_Income_Band,
                            levels = c("Low", "Mid", "High"),
                            ordered = TRUE),
    Form_Level = factor(Form_Level,
                        levels = c("JHS 1-2", "JHS 3-SHS 1", "SHS 2-3", "SHS 3+"),
                        ordered = TRUE),
    Bullying_Experienced = factor(Bullying_Experienced,
                                  levels = c("Never", "Sometimes", "Often"),
                                  ordered = TRUE),
    School_Level = factor(School_Level,
                          levels = c("JHS", "SHS", "Combined")),
    School_Type = factor(School_Type,
                         levels = c("Public", "Private", "Mission")),
    Urban_Rural = factor(Urban_Rural,
                         levels = c("Rural", "Peri-urban", "Urban"),
                         ordered = TRUE),
    Parent_Occupation = factor(Parent_Occupation),
    Orphan_Status = factor(Orphan_Status),
    Region = factor(Region),
    Passed_Core = factor(Passed_Core, levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    Sex = factor(Sex, levels = c("Female", "Male")),
    Residence_Type = factor(Residence_Type, levels = c("Day", "Boarding")),
    Internet_Access_School = factor(Internet_Access_School, levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    Has_Textbooks_All = factor(Has_Textbooks_All, levels = c("No", "Yes"))
  )
```

### Long-format subject scores for Task 3

The final cleaned dataset now contains the four subject scores required for the Task 3 visualisation. We therefore reshape these columns after `dat_clean` has been fully created and cleaned.

```{r create-scores-long}
# reshape from wide (four score columns) to long (one row per student per subject)
subject_scores_long <- dat_clean %>%
  select(Student_ID, School_Level, Sex, Form_Level, Passed_Core,
         English_Score, Mathematics_Score,
         Science_Score, Social_Studies_Score) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(English_Score, Mathematics_Score,
                  Science_Score, Social_Studies_Score),
    names_to  = "Subject",
    values_to = "Score"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # clean up the subject name - remove "_Score" and replace underscore with a space
    Subject = str_remove(Subject, "_Score"),
    Subject = str_replace(Subject, "_", " ")
  )

# check the dimensions
dim(subject_scores_long)
```

```{r scores-long-preview}
# show the first 10 rows
subject_scores_long %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Table 7: First 10 rows of subject_scores_long (long-format subject scores for Task 3 visualisation)")
```

The reshaped dataset has `r nrow(subject_scores_long)` rows four rows per student, one for
each subject. We will use this object in Task 3 to draw the faceted score comparison plot.
Some scores are NA (Mathematics and Science had 4% missingness which we kept in Task 1) -
those will be handled with `na.rm = TRUE` in Task 3.

```{r check-risk-level}
# check the Risk_Level distribution
dat_clean %>%
  count(Risk_Level)
```

```{r check-attendance-gap}
# quick check of the new Attendance_Gap variable
summary(dat_clean$Attendance_Gap)
```
